//: ABS stop that crosses from dry asphalt onto packed snow before
//1: the brake event.  Models a hard brake on packed snow -- friction
//2: limit is far below what the brake hardware can produce -- without
//3: ABS the wheels lock instantly and the car slides on whatever-mu,
//4: taking a long time to stop.  With ABS the wheels stay near the
//5: peak-slip point and actually decelerate close to the friction
//6: limit.  This is the scenario where ABS earns its keep -- stopping
//9: Launch and reach 15 m/s on the asphalt runway with the same
//10: throttle ramp as the other ABS scenarios (see abs_high_mu_stop.json)
//11: instead of launching on the slippery patch itself.  This vehicle's
//12: mass and weight split puts the front axle's traction ceiling on a
//13: low-mu surface well below what a normal launch needs regardless of
//14: throttle shape -- at the original mu=0.10 that ceiling was ~628 N
//15: (~0.49 m/s^2, ~31 s to 15 m/s even with an ideal traction-limited
//16: launch); at the current mu=0.20 it's roughly double that but still
//17: far slower than an asphalt launch (~15 s vs. ~6 s).  So the car
//18: accelerates on asphalt, then coasts across the asphalt/snow
//19: boundary and settles for ~2 s / ~30 m on the snow before the brake
//20: event, so the whole brake-and-ABS story this scenario tests
//21: happens on the slippery surface, not mid-transition or mid-launch.
//22: See level/flat_low_mu_transition.json for the runway geometry and
//23: the friction-value citation (0.20, hard-packed snow, not polished
name: abs_low_mu_stop

events.//: Ease onto the pedal over ~0.75 s instead of stepping to full
events.//1: throttle -- same ramp as the other ABS scenarios.
